title: Count Separate Networks
statement:
There are n machines, numbered 0 to n - 1, and a list of two-way cables edges, where edges[i] = [a, b] links machines a and b. Machines that can reach each other through any chain of cables belong to the same network.

Return the number of separate networks. A machine with no cables is a network on its own. The same pair may be linked by more than one cable.

examples.why: The networks are {0, 1, 2}, {3, 4} and {5}. Machine 5 has no cables, but it still counts.
After the first two cables there seem to be two groups, but the cable [1, 2] merges them. Labels handed out in input order must be able to merge later.
The formula n − (number of cables) gives 1, but the third cable closes a loop and joins nothing new. The answer is {0, 1, 2} and {3}.

hints: One way: count how many times you have to start a new search to reach every machine.

Another way: start with n separate networks. Each cable either merges two different networks (count goes down by 1) or links two machines already in the same one (nothing changes). How do you tell which, quickly?

Give each network a representative. Keep a parent pointer per machine and follow it to the root to find the representative. To merge, point one root at the other. Keep the trees flat with path compression and union by rank.

explain.intuition:
A search works: build the adjacency list, and every time you meet a machine no earlier search reached, start a BFS from it and add one. This problem is also the best place to learn a structure built for exactly this question, union-find (also called a disjoint-set union). It keeps machines grouped into sets and answers two things fast: find(x), "which set is x in?", and union(a, b), "merge the sets of a and b". Start with n sets of one machine each. For each cable, if find(a) !== find(b), merge them and lower the count by one. A cable inside one set is ignored, which is why example 3 is 2 and not 1.

Each set is a tree of parent pointers whose root is the set's representative. find walks up to the root. Two tricks keep those walks short. Union by rank: when merging, hang the shorter tree under the taller one (rank is an upper bound on height), so height grows only when two equal trees meet, and stays at most log n. Path compression: after find(x) reaches the root, point every node on the path straight at the root, so the next lookup is one step. Together they make each operation take amortised α(n) time, where α is the inverse Ackermann function: below 5 for any input that fits in the universe. Unlike BFS, union-find also works when cables arrive one at a time and you need the count after each one, a bit like grouping chat threads as reply links stream in.
steps: Create parent[i] = i and rank[i] = 0 for every machine, and set count = n.
find(x): walk up parents to the root, then walk the path again and point each node directly at the root.
union(a, b): find both roots. If they are equal, return false. Otherwise attach the root with the smaller rank under the other; if the ranks are equal, pick one and add 1 to its rank. Return true.
For each cable, if union(a, b) returns true, lower count by one.
pitfalls: Computing n - edges.length. Cables that close a loop (example 3) or repeat a pair do not merge anything.
Forgetting machines with no cables. They are networks of size one, as machine 5 in example 1.
Writing union as parent[a] = b on the machines instead of their roots. That cuts a out of its own set and silently splits networks.

complexity.time: O(n + edges · α(n)) with union-find; O(n + edges) with BFS
complexity.space: O(n) for union-find; O(n + edges) for BFS

solutions.title: BFS from each unvisited machine
solutions.idea: Build an adjacency list. Scan machines; each one no earlier search reached starts a new BFS and adds one to the count.

solutions.title: Union-find with path compression and union by rank
solutions.idea: Start with n sets. Each cable that joins two different sets merges them and lowers the count. Flat trees make every find nearly O(1).

followups: Cables arrive one at a time and you must report the count after each. Which solution handles that without starting over?
Cables can also be removed. Why is that hard for union-find, and what trick works if all the removals are known in advance?
